title: The Secret of the Shimmering Badge
markdown:
On Willow Creek the houses stood shoulder to shoulder like old friends, windows lit in pairs, gardens arguing politely about roses. Pip and Posy, twins bright as a long afternoon, kept a secret that only their scruffy terrier, Perrin, was officially allowed to know. They were founders, investigators, and slightly self-appointed guardians of the Nocturnal Society. Perrin’s tail did the minutes.

Their club met in a hollow oak at the park’s edge. Moonlight came through in coins. The air smelled of damp earth and old wood, a smell that meant safety and midnight. On a velvet cushion, soft as a whisper, rested the Lumina Badge. It held a quiet inner light, needed for the Midnight Muster the next night, and it made even ordinary pebbles in their collection look like they were trying harder.

“Perrin, fetch the Lumina Badge, if you please,” Pip said. His voice stayed calm on the surface. He hated being laughed at, ever since Mrs Higgins’s prize poodle, a balloon, and a story the street still told. Oddly, he could still make people laugh when a plan needed it. His spectacles slid down his nose as if they had somewhere better to be.

Perrin trotted over, nudged the cushion, and whined. The velvet was empty.

Posy’s laugh, which usually arrived first, stopped in her throat. She had been lining up interesting pebbles; her fingers were still dusty. “It’s gone.” A shiver that was not cold went down her back.

They did not panic, not in any useful sense. Posy counted to three, which she did when jokes would not come. Pip opened his leather notebook, smudged fingerprints and all. “Rule one. Assess the scene. Observe. Deduce. Do not chase squirrels.” That last was for Perrin, who had a professional interest in the park’s chatter.

The only clue was a feather so fine it might have been a cobweb with ambitions. It spoke of lightness and hurry, as if the thief had left by air.

A scrabble at the entrance, and Flicker tumbled in, all limbs and apology. He had joined last week, drawn by midnight-mission stories, a boy of nervous giggles and shoes that plotted against him.

“Terribly sorry. I was just checking the badge. For the Muster. Making sure it was… badge-worthy.” His smile wobbled. His face was strawberry-pink.

Pip’s eyes narrowed. Flicker had been peculiar all week: louder giggles, a gaze that bolted, a lantern nearly dropped, laces knotted into a permanent sculpture. “Flicker. Where is the Lumina Badge?”

Flicker’s hands clenched. “I don’t know. I saw it, and then—” He went into a hinge-squeak of laughter that sounded less like guilt than like a person coming unscrewed.

Posy saw the rest. As Flicker stood, he nearly met a root. A tiny pair of spectacles, too small for any human nose, slipped from his pocket, silvery, almost not there. He snatched them. His “check” earlier that evening had been a dash.

“Pip,” Posy murmured. “He went somewhere. Perrin can follow.”

Perrin thumped the bark once and trotted for the park gate, nose busy. Posy followed. Pip took a last look at the empty cushion, notebook in hand, and went after them.

The park at night was another country. Old trees threw long shadows across dewy grass, and the bandstand’s peeling paint looked like someone had started a letter and given up. The wind in the leaves sounded like secrets that had agreed to share. Jasmine and wet soil hung in the air, and somewhere a late bird argued with itself. Pip lifted his small torch. Dust motes turned in the beam like a handful of slow stars. For a few breaths nobody spoke. Even Perrin waited, as if the light had asked for manners. A moth wrote a small signature on the beam and left. Posy, who usually filled quiet with a joke, let this one stay empty. Pip wrote nothing in the notebook, which for him was almost a poem.

Then the terrier’s yips led them to the bandstand, paint peeling like old postcards. Flicker stood there, making a wilted dandelion bob as if it were a very small orchestra. He muttered to it.

“Flicker,” Pip called. “We know you took the badge.”

The dandelion flew. Flicker looked cornered down to his socks. “I did. Not really. I was trying to keep it safe.”

Safe from a phantom bird? A rogue badger?

He breathed as if cookies were about to be confessed. “There’s a glow-worm. Very shy. It lives by the bandstand. It likes the Lumina Badge. It keeps trying to borrow it. I’ve been distracting it. With my secret glow-worm magic.” He wiggled the next dandelion. “It’s silly. The badge is so bright, and the worm gets excited, and if it took the badge too far it would get lost. It gets lonely, I think.”

They looked where he pointed. In the damp grass by the crumbling steps, a tiny light pulsed, lonely and polite.

Flicker had not stolen anything. He had run a comical guard for a creature that wanted to borrow the sun.

Pip knelt. He took the Lumina Badge from his own pocket—retrieved from the grass where Flicker’s “magic” had parked it, still faintly warm—and held it out. The badge answered. The glow-worm brightened, a small conversation in two colours. Perrin offered a soft woof of official approval.

Posy nudged Flicker. “For a silly secret, it worked. That worm may think you are theatre.”

Flicker’s giggle came up from his toes, unforced. The glow-worm blinked once, which would have to do for thanks.

They walked the badge home to the oak along the same dewy grass, cushion restored, Muster still possible. Flicker was allowed to sit nearer the velvet, the tiny spectacles returned to his pocket for the worm’s next visit. He practised a dandelion bow that made Posy snort and Pip pretend not to smile. Pip wrote a new rule that was not quite a rule: sometimes the clue is kindness wearing a squeaky laugh. He underlined do not chase squirrels twice, because Perrin was listening. Posy lined the pebbles again, leaving a gap for a glow-worm-shaped one if they ever found it. Perrin, second-in-command, put his chin on the roots and slept as if the night had been filed.

The Midnight Muster went ahead under a moon that did not ask for explanations. Members arrived with pebbles, jokes, and one carefully carried dandelion. The Lumina Badge shone no brighter than before, which was enough. On Willow Creek the houses kept standing together, and the oak kept its smell of earth and wood, and a shy light by the bandstand waited, some nights, for a dandelion to conduct.
characters: Pip and Posy (bold twins), Perrin (a steadfast terrier)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic mystery adventure for older children
